name: Invergordon
title: Invergordon Rig and Ship UTM | Cromarty Firth Gauging
description: Thickness gauging at Invergordon for drilling rigs, offshore vessels, cruise ships and wind installation ships in the Cromarty Firth: UT, MPI and piping.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement in the Cromarty Firth at Invergordon
intro: Invergordon sits on the north shore of the Cromarty Firth, a deep and sheltered inlet off the Moray Firth that has been receiving drilling rigs for inspection, repair and maintenance since 1978. The same waters now host offshore wind installation vessels, decommissioning units and a busy summer cruise season. Rigs and ships moored in the firth for weeks at a time suit full gauging and crack-detection programmes, and our technicians come out from India to the unit or vessel for each one.

highlights.h: Rigs in the firth for repair
highlights.p: Semi-submersibles and jack-ups come into the Cromarty Firth between contracts for inspection, repair and maintenance, some of them for weeks. That time suits gauging of pontoons, columns and preload tanks, and crack detection at bracing nodes and leg chords.

Installation vessels, cargo ships carrying turbine components and units preparing for decommissioning work use the firth's quays at Invergordon and Nigg. Deck strength, crane foundations and sea-fastening attachments are the usual focus after a season of heavy loading.

highlights.h: Cruise calls in the summer season
highlights.p: Invergordon is a busy cruise port, with ships berthing so passengers can explore the Highlands. A cruise call is short, but external piping and deck readings can be planned for the hours alongside, and the ship's technical team can open tanks in advance.

port.h: The Cromarty Firth: a sheltered deep-water firth for rigs and ships
p: The Cromarty Firth opens to the Moray Firth through a narrow entrance between the two headlands known as the Sutors, and widens inside into a long, deep basin protected from North Sea weather. Invergordon lies on its northern shore, with Nigg near the entrance on the same side and the village of Cromarty on the southern headland. The Port of Cromarty Firth is the trust port responsible for the harbour, providing pilotage and running the quays at Invergordon, while the Port of Nigg near the entrance is a separate private port, which Mitsui and Mitsui O.S.K. Lines bought from Global Energy Group in 2025. Deep water close inshore lets large units moor in the firth itself, not only at the quays, so rigs and ships can lie here for long periods in shelter.

Drilling rigs are the firth's signature traffic. Semi-submersibles and jack-ups have come here for inspection, repair and maintenance since the late 1970s, and the port recorded its 750th rig visit in 2024. Rigs arrive between drilling contracts, after plug-and-abandonment campaigns or before reactivation, and some leave for recycling: in early 2026 the semi-submersible Stena Spey was towed from the firth to Turkey for decommissioning. Offshore wind has added installation and construction vessels and the cargo ships that bring turbine components, with marshalling and fabrication work at Nigg and Invergordon serving projects offshore. Offshore supply and anchor-handling vessels support both the rig work and the wind farms, and come alongside between duties. Each visit brings its own mix of contractors, from repair crews to the inspection teams working through the owner's survey list.

Invergordon is also one of Scotland's leading cruise ports, with ships berthing through the summer so passengers can reach Inverness, Loch Ness and the wider Highlands. The firth is part of the Inverness and Cromarty Firth Green Freeport, intended to bring renewable energy manufacturing and hydrogen projects to its shores. Seasonal patterns follow the trades: cruise calls concentrate between spring and autumn, wind installation work favours the summer weather window, and rig visits come whenever contracts end. Winters are dark and windy, but the firth itself stays workable, so a rig or vessel moored inside it can usually be inspected even when conditions in the open North Sea are poor. The same quays may see a cruise ship one day and a rig's supply vessel the next.

facilities.h: Where gauging happens in the Cromarty Firth
p: Rigs are worked in two ways. Jack-ups can be brought alongside or jacked up close to the quays, while semi-submersibles are usually moored in the deep water of the firth, with crews and contractors reaching them by boat. A rig in for repair and maintenance has its own power, lighting and accommodation, and its preload, ballast and drill-water tanks can be emptied in sequence for gauging while other contractors carry out their work. Pontoon and column structure, bracings and the connections between them are where fatigue and corrosion meet, so thickness readings are paired with magnetic particle testing on cleaned welds at the nodes the owner's inspection plan identifies.

Ships use the quays at Invergordon and the Port of Nigg. Offshore vessels supporting the rigs and the wind farms come alongside between duties, and cargo and installation ships stay for days while components are loaded or discharged. Vessels needing a docking for a renewal survey usually go to yards elsewhere in the UK or on the Continent, and a period in the Cromarty Firth before that docking is a convenient time for pre-docking readings. Cruise ships at Invergordon are short calls, best used for external piping and deck work arranged in advance with the ship's technical staff.
list: Semi-submersible moorings in the firth — pontoon, column and ballast tank gauging plus MPI at bracing nodes during repair and maintenance periods.
Invergordon quays — jack-up preload tank and leg structure checks, and deck and tank gauging on offshore support vessels between duties.
Port of Nigg quays — deck, crane-foundation and sea-fastening inspection on installation and cargo ships handling heavy components.
Invergordon cruise berths — external piping and deck readings on cruise ships during summer calls, with tanks opened in advance by the crew.
Rigs preparing for tow-out — condition gauging on towing points and hull structure before a unit leaves for a new contract or recycling.

context.h: Rig class surveys, offshore wind and the UK regulatory frame
p: Mobile offshore drilling units are classed and surveyed much like ships, but under rules written for their structure: special periodic surveys every five years include thickness measurement of pontoons, columns, legs and the members the class society treats as critical, along with close examination of welded joints. Many owners use a stay in the Cromarty Firth to bring this work forward, or to check the structure before a unit is reactivated after a period stacked. The offshore safety regime enforced by the Health and Safety Executive in UK waters, and the owner's own structural integrity plans, add further reasons to know the condition of steel before the unit returns to work.

Ships calling at Invergordon and Nigg come under Maritime and Coastguard Agency port state control, which the UK carries out within the Paris MoU. Offshore support and wind vessels here sail under a mix of national and open registers, and the wind market in particular expects documented hull and deck condition from the vessels it charters. Units leaving the firth for recycling, as the Stena Spey did, bring the UK's ship recycling rules into play, including the expectation of an Inventory of Hazardous Materials, so owners selling older tonnage often want a condition record made before the tow.

jobs.h: Typical gauging and NDT jobs at Invergordon
jobs.p: Most Cromarty Firth work is planned around a rig or vessel that will be here long enough to do it properly. We coordinate with the owner's rig manager or superintendent and with the other contractors on board, so that tank cleaning, access and permits are lined up before the team arrives and gauging does not hold up repair work. Where a unit is preparing for a contract or a survey, we prioritise the structure the class surveyor and the client will look at first, and report each reading against the unit's drawings so the next survey can build on it. Short calls by cruise and cargo ships get a tighter scope fixed in advance.
list: Pontoon and column ballast tank gauging on a semi-submersible moored in the firth after a plug-and-abandonment campaign, ahead of its next contract.
Jack-up preload tank gauging and MPI on leg chords and spudcan connections during a repair period alongside at Invergordon.
Deck and crane-pedestal inspection on an offshore wind installation vessel after a season of heavy component lifts.
Towing bracket and hull condition gauging on a rig preparing to leave the firth under tow.
External UT of sea-water and fuel piping on a cruise ship during a summer call, scoped in advance with the chief engineer.

logistics: Inverness Airport, with connections to London, other UK cities and some European hubs, is the nearest arrival point, and Invergordon is reached from there by road. Aberdeen and Edinburgh airports are alternatives with more international routes, followed by rail or road north. The team travels from India on UK visas, so we ask for a rig's or vessel's expected time in the firth as early as possible. Quay passes, boat transfers to moored rigs and site inductions are arranged through the agent, the port and the rig owner before the team arrives.
vessels: Offshore wind installation and construction vessels

faqs.q: Can you gauge a semi-submersible moored in the Cromarty Firth?
faqs.a: Yes. A semi-submersible in for repair and maintenance usually has power, lighting and accommodation running, so the team works from the rig and reaches it by boat. Pontoon and column tanks are emptied, ventilated and certified for entry in a sequence agreed with the rig manager, and bracing nodes are cleaned for magnetic particle testing alongside the thickness readings.

faqs.q: Do you inspect jack-up rigs at Invergordon?
faqs.a: Yes. On a jack-up the priorities are usually preload and ballast tanks in the hull, the leg chords and bracing where they pass through the jackcase, and spudcan connections where they can be reached. We combine ultrasonic thickness readings with magnetic particle testing on cleaned welds, and report against the unit's drawings so the owner and the class surveyor can see where repair is needed.

faqs.q: Can a cruise ship be gauged during a call at Invergordon?
faqs.a: A cruise call allows a limited scope. External UT on engine-room piping, deck lines and scrubber wash-water and overboard piping can be done during the hours alongside if it is planned with the chief engineer, and tanks the crew has emptied beforehand can be entered. Larger programmes are better kept for a docking, with our readings feeding the yard's work list.

faqs.q: What about vessels working on offshore wind projects from Nigg?
faqs.a: Installation and cargo vessels carrying turbine components take heavy deck loads and crane forces, and sea-fastenings are welded on and cut away repeatedly. Deck plating, the structure under load spreaders, crane pedestals and sea-fastening attachment points are the usual scope, combining thickness readings with crack detection. Work is fitted between load-outs so the vessel's schedule is not held up.

faqs.q: Can a rig be inspected before it is towed away for recycling or a new contract?
faqs.a: Yes. Before a tow, owners and the marine warranty surveyor want to know the condition of towing brackets, fairleads and the hull structure around them, and a buyer or recycler may want a condition baseline. A short gauging and crack-detection scope at those points can be done while the rig is still moored in the firth, with the readings referenced to the unit's drawings.
